Everything is computed on your phone. Motion data never leaves it; your location only leaves it rounded to about 50 km, to fetch NASA's satellite picture of your region.
Lay your phone flat on a table
Screen up, hands off, away from laptops and magnets. Hold still until the first dot fills, then give it a quarter turn on the table and hold again: four times.
Why four? The gyroscope knows exactly how far you turned. If the compass disagrees, something nearby is bending it, and averaging four directions cancels the phone's own magnetic bias.
View held. Drag to move. Pinch out to follow the phone again.
Drawn from measured star positions and computed planets. Not a photograph. · No motion sensors: drag to aim
Drag the sky until one thing you can see (the Moon, a planet, a bright star) sits where you see it.
Aim the big gold crosshair at it.
. North is then set from what you see, and from then on the gyroscope alone keeps it: no more compass drift. The teal markers show where WANDERERS currently thinks landmarks are.

Motion: the gyroscope drives every movement; the compass only sets north, averaged while the phone lies flat and corrected slowly after (sensor fusion, tested on simulated noisy sensors: 0.1–0.5° error, 0.1° wobble). Sky: J2000 positions precessed to today (IAU 1976), UTC time and Earth's rotation (IAU 1982 sidereal time) at your GPS position, refraction (Saemundsson). Magnetic north to true north: NOAA/BGS World Magnetic Model 2025. Earth imagery: NASA Blue Marble and Black Marble via NASA GIBS. Cities: GeoNames.
